Potted specimen of a complete adult southern marsupial mole or itjaritjari (Notoryctes typhlops). The specimen is preserved in fluid and contained in a rectangular, glass battery jar. The southern marsupial mole is found in central Australian desert habitats. It is a true marsupial, and its similarity to placental European moles is a result of evolutionary convergence. It is likely this specimen was produced from animals collected in central South Australia and received by Professor of Anatomy Frederic Wood Jones during his time at the University of Adelaide. Wood Jones was being sent many specimens at this time from Anthony Gladstone Bolam, stationmaster at Ooldea and a collector of animals which he obtained through the assistance of local Aboriginal collectors.
source_reference_tsim: 9.2.1010, Wood Jones number

description_tsim: This model was manufactured in the late 19th century by anatomist Daniel John Cunningham (1850-1909) and model makers Casciani and Son of Dublin. This is one of three such models in the Harry Brookes Allen Museum collection. This model was figured in Cunningham's 'Contribution to the surface anatomy of the cerebral hemispheres' published in 1892 in Dublin. The caption describes this model as the 'head of an old man aged seventy-five years'. For this study, Cunningham produced molds for 'twenty-two models of the human head, one of the orang, one of the chimpanzee, one of the baboon, two of the Macacque, and one of [capuchin monkey]'.

Plaster model of brain section, larger than life size, mounted on a black wooden board. The model was produced by Jules Talriche, a Parisian anatomical model maker active in the second half of the 19th century. An original cardboard label describes the model (in French) as, 'Inferior surface of the encephalon, a segment of the anterior and posterior lobes has been removed to show the cerebral extension of the protuberance, the origin of the optic nerve, the lower portion of the corpus striatum, etc.'
Plaster model of dissected brain mounted on wooden base.

Plaster model of an oversized alligator brain manufactured by Deyrolle of Paris. The species is described as 'Alligator lucius', a now superceded scientfic name for the American alligator. Part of a comparative set of eight models, comprising brains of a frog, ammocoete (lamprey larva), alligator, shark, rabbit, dog, trout, and pigeon.

description_tsim: Plaster cast of a human skull from Cro-Magnon, an upper paleolithic fossil site in southwestern France. This skull, named 'Cro-Magnon 2', was discovered in the 1860s and is thought to be a female. This site, discovered in 1868, yielded fossils of anatomically modern humans that have been dated to 27,680 years before present. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in c.1909 to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

description_tsim: Plaster cast of a partial left humerus from a Neanderthal (Homo neanderthalensis). This bone was part of the first fossil discoveries in the Neander Valley in 1856; an assemblage of bones comprising a partial skull, a fragment of the right scapula, a right clavicle, both humerus (the right side complete), a complete right radius, fragments of right and left forearm bones, five ribs, an almost complete left half of the pelvis and both femora. The skull from this assemblage has been dated at ~40,000 years old and is the type specimen for the Neanderthal species. The description of these bones published in 1864 and the recogition that they represented a distinct, ancient species of extinct human marked a paradigm shift in scientific thinking. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in the early 1900s to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

Resin cast of the skull of Australopithecus afarensis. A. afarensis is the best represented early hominid with approximately 300 individuals representing the species. The australopithecines are only known from Africa; none have ever been found in Europe or Asia. They had ape-like and human-like characteristics. Like apes, australopithecines had long arms with curved fingers, a flat nose and strong jaw with a cranial capacity ranging from 375 to 500cc. Like humans, they had small canine teeth and had a lower body capable of bipedal walking. This full-size skull was sculpted for Bone Clones by scientific sculptor Steven Wagner. It is a generalized representation of a male afarensis—not reflective of any one specimen.
Complete pelvic girdle from a common wombat (Vombatus ursinus).
Complete disarticulated skeleton, with intact skull and mandible, of a koala (Phascolarctos cinereus). Additional small box containing small bones included and a heavy metal '36' tile.

This specimen was collected by the McCoy Society on their expedition to Bass Strait's King Island from December 6th 1937 to January 26th 1938.

description_tsim: Plaster cast of a left temporal bone fragment from a Neanderthal (Homo neanderthalensis). This bone was part of a fossil assemblage discovered in Krapina, Croatia between 1899 and 1905. These Neanderthal fossils have been dated at 120-130 thousand years old and represent one of the largest assemblages of Upper Pleistocene human skeletal remains ever found. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in the early 1900s to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

Eight calculi mounted in a resin block. A calculus is a concretion of material, usually mineral salts, that forms in an organ or duct of the body.

Plaster teaching model of left upper third molar of a thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus). Mounted on black painted metal post fixed to black painted wooden base with paper label nailed on. The different morphological elements of the teeth are colour coded. The Henry Forman Atkinson Dental Museum holds six plaster models of thylacine teeth made by Professor Charles Harold Down in the 1930s at the request of Dr. E. D. Brooke Nicholls, lecturer in Comparative Dental Anatomy at the Dental School of the University of Melbourne. The thylacine tooth models comprise four left lower third molars (HFA2420, HFA2880, HFA2914, HFA4011) and two left upper third molars (HFA2879, HFA4010). The models are part of a sequence of nine marsupial species intended to illustrate the evolution of cusp formation, the thylacine being the most derived extant carnivorous marsupial dentition. Down’s description of his methodology indicates that he had firsthand access to the teeth he was reproducing. It is probable that Down referred to and moulded the teeth from the skull held by the Henry Forman Atkinson Dental Museum (HFA3795), as the left upper third and left lower third molars - and no other teeth - of that specimen appear to have been removed and then glued back into the skull.

description_tsim: The modern era of forensic odontology commenced with the identification of the victims of the Bazar de la Charité fire, which occurred on May 4, 1897 in Rue Jean-Goujon, Paris. 126 members of the Parisian aristocracy perished after an ether-oxygen film projector ignited a rapidly destructive fire. All but 30 of the victims were identified visually or by personal effects, on the day after the fire. The Paraguan Consul, Mr Albert Haus suggested consulting the dentists who had treated the remaining missing persons. One of the unidentified victims was the Duchesse d’Alencon who was a daughter of the Duke of Bavaria and sister of Elisabeth, Empress of Austria and Anne, Queen of Naples.  Dr Isaac B Davenport had provided dental services to the duchess and many of the other victims. He was a trained botanist as well as a dentist and his detailed notes included excellent drawings of the dentition. He examined the majority of the remaining unidentified bodies, and a number of other dentists were invited to examine the remains of the deceased. Eventually all but five of the victims were able to be identified. The police accepted these dental identifications and released the bodies to the families.

On his return to Australia Storey commenced working as a Research Fellow in the Department of Pathology in the University of Melbourne and later becoming Dean of the Dental Faculty 1971-1973 and 1979-1981, and subsequently the Inaugural Dean of Child Dental Health. In the 1960’s and 70’s Tony developed strong academic collaborations with University of Melbourne academics in bone calcium metabolism such as Professor Jack Martin, Professor Roger Mellick and Dr. David McCredie, this led him, among other projects, to investigate the staining of teeth in young children caused by tetracycline drugs, leading to physicians ceasing to prescribe to young children. In the late 1970’s, with the support of his brother Haddon Storey, (Victorian State Attorney General at that time) legislation was introduced to support the fluoridation of Melbourne’s water supply which resulted in a dramatic reduction in dental caries.  Sir Gordon Roy Cameron obtained his MBBS from the University of Melbourne in 1922. For the following 2 years Dr Cameron was the University of Melbourne Stewart lecturer in pathology and lecturer in general pathology in the Dental Faculty.  In 1937 Dr Cameron was appointed Professor of Pathology at the University College Hospital in London in 1937. A copy of Sir Roy Cameron's obituary 15th October 1966 from the British Medical Journal was inside the book.

description_tsim: Annie Jean Macnamara (1899-1968) was a determined and outspoken clinician who successfully combined research, a busy clinical practice and a strong commitment to her patients. She was widely recognised, receiving a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1935 for her outstanding contribution to the care of polio sufferers.  She graduated in 1922 from the University of Melbourne with an MBBS and the Beaney scholarship in surgery, and began her internship at the Melbourne Hospital.  It was after gaining a residency at the Children's Hospital that she first encountered the devastating consequences of polio, and she henceforth dedicated the majority of her career to the treatment and rehabilitation of children suffering from the disease. With Macfarlane Burnet she discovered that there was more than one strain of the polio virus. A fellowship in orthopaedics in the United States honed her skills in physical treatment, and she adapted splints and devices to immobilise, protect and subsequently allow rehabilitation of paralysed limbs. She is also credited with ordering Australia's first artificial respirator during her time overseas.

description_tsim: Two photographs, right view and left view. Stereoscopy is a technique for creating or enhancing the illusion of depth in an image by means of stereopsis for binocular vision. Originally, stereogram referred to a pair of stereo images which could be viewed using a stereoscope. Most stereoscopic methods present a pair of two-dimensional images to the viewer. The left image is presented to the left eye and the right image is presented to the right eye. When viewed, the human brain perceives the images as a single 3D view, giving the viewer the perception of 3D depth. Skiagrapher was the term used for a radiographer until the end of the First World War. In the early days, a skiagram, (or skiagraph), was the term used for a radiograph.  Alfred  George Fryett was born in 1862 in Lewisham London. After arriving Melbourne about 1893, Fryett was among the first to use X-rays in the late 1890s, assisting at the Melbourne Hospital. Fryett also worked with surgeon Fredric Dougan Bird at Clareton Hospital and with Harry Brookes Allen, Professor of Anatomy and Pathology in the University of Melbourne. In 1901 the University of Melbourne purchased X-ray equipment under the direction of Professor Allen. In 1902 Fryett was employed by Allen to prepare specimens with opaque injections and produce this collection of skigrams which display the aterirs throughout the human body. After Bird closed Claremont Hospital in 1914, Fryett returned to England and joined the R.A.M.C working as a radiographer at Lady Dudley's Hospital. The Sands and McDougall Melbourne Directories list Fryett as having his own radio-diagnostic business ," A.G. Fryett,  X-ray Department , 41 Spring St" from 1916 to 1919. In 1919 or 1920 Fryett returned to London, suffering health problems and retired in Malborough with his wife.  Fryett like many other pionerrs in this field became an x-ray ' martyr' dying in England in 1930, the result of 'carcinoma of the axillaand lung; epithelioma of hands; x-ray burns of fingers and hands'. Like other early radiographers or 'Skiagraphists', Fryett would often use his own  hands to test the strenght of x-ray beams, instead of using photometers that could easily be mislaid.  The collection of sterio skiagrams is Fryett's work in the Anatomy department, University of Melbourne from 1902 to c. 1914.

description_tsim: Presented to Dr Herbert M. Hewlett (1872-1957) by Dr William Snowball (1854–1902); attributed as a 'fine set' by Professor Harold D. Attwood (1928-2005).  Hewlett was educated at Alexander Sutherland's Carlton College. After three years of a medical course at the University of Melbourne he completed his degree at the Edinburgh Medical School, graduating with distinctions in all subjects of the final year (M.R.C.P., 1896). He was greatly influenced by his teachers at Edinburgh, particularly the noted paediatrician Dr John Thomson. Hewlett had been keenly interested in reports of Röntgen's discovery of X-rays in November 1895 and closely followed developments in the field.  Hewlett returned to Melbourne in 1896 and joined his father's practice. Late that year he was appointed to the honorary staff of the Children's Hospital. There, because of long-standing interest in electricity and photography he was invited to install X-ray equipment costing some £25, and thus in 1897 established the first radiology department in a Melbourne public hospital. He served the Children's Hospital for thirty-eight years. For the first fifteen years his duties combined those of honorary physician, surgeon and radiologist. In 1912 he was appointed skiagraphist, from then on confining his interests to radiology. He was also appointed skiagraphist at St Vincent's Hospital from 1911 until 1934.

description_tsim: Small brass plaque with two holes at each end, engraved with the words "PROFESSOR GEORGE BRITTON HALFORD". Possibly a name plate used for the door of Professor Halford's office at the Melbourne Medical School.  Professor Halford (1824-1910) was the School's first professor of anatomy, pathology and physiology.  It was 1 May 1863 when George Britton Halford (1824–1910) started as the first professor of anatomy, physiology and pathology, at the Medical School. There were three students, Patrick Moloney (1843-1904), Alexander Mackie(1839-1892) and William Carey Rees (1843–1879), and classes were held in a shed erected at the back of Professor Halford’s private rooms.  In 1876 the faculty of medicine was established and took over administration of courses from the Medical School Committee. Halford was elected Dean and held office until 1886 and again in 1890-96.  Halford recommended as early as 1871, while president of the professorial board, that women who passed the relevant examinations sign the matriculation book should be admitted to the University of Melbourne. However, Vice-Chancellor A.C. Brownless’s (1817–1897) view of university education did not extend to the inclusion of women; he actively opposed the motion to admit women to the University of Melbourne in 1879, and to admit women to medicine in 1887.

description_tsim: A small, mold-made brown glass bottle used to hold Morses Indian Root Pills, which claimed to cleanse the blood and were sold by W.H. Comstock Company Pty. Ltd. in Australia. Comstock's Morses Indian Root Pills were first manufactured by the American firm in the mid-1850’s but their popularity peaked in Australia in the 1920’s. Indian root is likely Wahoo (Euonymus atropurpureus), a common herb in Native American medicine used as a laxative. One of the most popular patent medicines, Dr. Morse's Indian Root Pills was almost identical to the hundreds of other cure-alls, or at least claimed to cure the most common ailments of the day. It was advertised as a specific cure for most blood, stomach and liver diseases. The manufacturers claimed that the pills would "absolutely remove all dyspepsia, giddiness, headache, and are most useful in female disorders." (ref. Hagley Museum)
